summary: Explains that renumbering routers involves more than addresses and routes, since routers interact with servers such as DNS and SNMP. It is an informational guide to the things to consider.

plainLanguage.summary: Changing network addresses affects routers and other services that store those addresses. RFC 2072 helps network teams inventory the changes and plan the transition.

subtitle: A planning guide to the router settings and network services affected when IP addresses change.

tldr.problem: Changing an organization's IP addresses affects more than router interfaces. Router settings and network services can also contain addresses that must change.
tldr.mechanism: The guide explains how to scope the address changes, reduce hard-coded addresses, inspect router features, and plan a staged transition with backups and a retreat plan.
tldr.outcome: This is an Informational planning guide, not a protocol. It has been updated by RFC 4192.

today: RFC 2072 is an Informational guide and has been updated by RFC 4192.

sections.title: Plan the Renumbering Before Changing Addresses
sections.content:
RFC 2072 covers router-related planning after an organization has decided to renumber some or all of its IP address space. The guide recommends starting with a clear reason for the change, understanding the current and planned numbering, identifying pitfalls, and preparing a transition plan.

Routers are not the only affected devices. Bridges, switches, and infrastructure servers such as DNS and SNMP may also interact with the address plan. The guide is intended to be vendor-independent, but it notes that not every router implements every feature it discusses.
sections.plainLanguage: Start by deciding what addresses will change and why. Then check every device and service that uses those addresses, not only the routers.

sections.title: Prefixes Define the Scope
sections.content:
A router examines the leftmost bits of a destination IP address, called a prefix, and looks for that prefix in its routing table. The prefix may be controlled by an outside organization, by the enterprise, or by both. A change to the provider-assigned part has a different scope from a change to the internal subnetting.

The guide recommends an inventory of prefixes that will remain unchanged, be renumbered, be retired, or be added. Renumbering is easier when each old prefix maps to one new prefix, but old and new address space may need to coexist during a transition. The guide says effects are often greatest higher in a routing hierarchy and least in stub networks.
sections.plainLanguage: A prefix is the part of an address that routers use to choose where traffic goes. List which prefixes will stay, change, or disappear so you can see which routers and networks are affected.

sections.title: Make Configurations Easier to Change
sections.content:
Before changing addresses, reduce the number of places where they are hard-coded. The guide recommends using default routes where suitable, summarizing routes, and referring to servers by DNS name rather than by IP address when the router supports it. Configuration changes may be easier to prepare on a server and then download to routers.

DNS does not remove every dependency. Routers may cache names, and configuration files may store fixed name-to-address mappings. Dynamic address assignment can reduce manual changes. Network address translation can reduce the amount of renumbering, but the guide warns that it can interfere with protocols that carry IP addresses inside their data.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep addresses in as few places as possible. Names and dynamic assignment can help, but caches and fixed settings still need attention, and translation can affect some protocols.

sections.title: Check Routing and Addressing Assumptions
sections.content:
The guide warns that some routers and hosts do not handle classless prefixes consistently. A network may need routers and routing protocols that support arbitrary prefix lengths. A classful routing protocol can also make discontiguous parts of the same address space appear ambiguous to another router.

Other problems can arise from filters, firewalls, router identifiers, interface masks, neighbor mappings, routing peers, management servers, and caches. The guide advises evaluating each router mechanism that stores or uses an affected address, including security filters that must remain correct during coexistence.
sections.plainLanguage: Older equipment may make assumptions about address classes that do not fit the new plan. Check routing protocols, filters, and neighbor settings before the change.

sections.title: Inventory, Back Up, and Cut Over
sections.content:
The transition plan starts with inventories of affected addresses and names. It then identifies topology changes, temporary address space, tools, and preparations that make future renumbering easier. Before the cutover, the guide says to take final backups of router configurations and DNS zone files.

The cutover may be phased or total. The plan should account for old and new addresses coexisting, DNS and firewall changes, cache clearing or restarts, and coordination with providers and partners. Changing one part of a routing hierarchy at a time can help limit instability. A retreat plan is needed in case major problems develop.
sections.plainLanguage: Make a complete list, back up the current settings, and decide how to recover if the change fails. A staged change can limit how much of the network is affected at once.
